questions.prompt: Which best describes an Advanced Persistent Threat (APT)?

options.text: A well-funded, skilled, patient adversary targeting a specific organization over time
A low-skill attacker running tools written by others
A single piece of self-spreading malware

questions.explanation: APTs are advanced, persistent, well-resourced adversaries (often nation-state-linked) that pursue a specific target over a long period.

questions.prompt: The sum of all points where an attacker could try to get in or get data out is called the attack ____.
questions.explanation: The attack surface is the total of all exposed points; reducing it (closing ports, removing services) cuts the number of possible attack vectors.

questions.prompt: Which are common types of threat actor? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Cybercriminals, insiders, and hacktivists are threat actors; a firewall is a defensive control, not an actor.

questions.prompt: Order the stages by which a weakness becomes an incident.
questions.explanation: Incidents progress from a vulnerability, to an exploit of it, to a compromise/foothold, to the eventual impact.

questions.prompt: Match each reference to what it provides.

pairs.right: Knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques
A vulnerability with no available patch yet

questions.explanation: ATT&CK catalogs adversary behavior, a CVE names a specific vulnerability, a CWE names the weakness type, and a zero-day is an unpatched flaw.

questions.prompt: Why can even a small, 'uninteresting' organization be compromised?

options.text: Most attacks are automated and opportunistic, hitting anything reachable and vulnerable
Only hand-picked targets are ever attacked
Small organizations have no attack surface
Attackers avoid systems they don't recognize

questions.explanation: Bots scan the whole internet for known weaknesses regardless of who owns the system — being reachable and vulnerable is enough.
